title: Integration of Biomechanics and Digital Technology: Using Kinovea for Motion Analysis and Learning for Beginner Athletes
authors: Muhammad Nur Hudha; Riezky Maya Probosari; Annisa Nur Khasanah; Supurwoko; Salsabila Kholifahtun Nisa’; Gifran Rihla Gifarka Latief
journal: Journal of Coaching and Sports Science
abstract: Background: The integration of biomechanics with digital motion-analysis technologies has introduced new approaches for examining movement efficiency, kinematic characteristics, and technical patterns in walking and running activities. Kinovea, as an accessible motion-analysis software, provides both visual and quantitative feedback. However, its application in supporting technique development among beginner athletes remains insufficiently explored. Aim: This study aims to describe the use of Kinovea in biomechanics training and examine its contribution to the awareness of kinematic characteristics and movement techniques among beginner athletes. Methods: A descriptive qualitative design involved 72 beginner athletes aged 18–25 years selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected over 16 weeks through interviews, field observations, and motion video recordings analyzed using Kinovea. Kinematic data focused on joint angles, stride behavior, and movement phases during walking, running, and the flight phase. Qualitative data were analyzed using content analysis with NVivo 12, while kinematic results were interpreted descriptively to identify performance patterns and areas for technical refinement. Result: Kinematic analysis showed coordinated joint-angle patterns across all phases. Walking analysis identified arm swing angles of 50.9°–58.8° and leg separation angles of 64.3°–67.2°, indicating a stable gait rhythm. The running analysis revealed knee angles of 68.8°–69.8° and elbow angles of 87.6°–89.1°, indicating efficient propulsive mechanics. The flight phase demonstrated knee angles of 81.2°–87.8° and elbow angles of 80.4°–88.3°, suggesting effective momentum use and postural stability. These measurements supported stride-efficiency assessment and technique evaluation. Qualitative findings revealed that Kinovea enabled athletes to interpret movement phases and identify technical inefficiencies through slow-motion and frame-by-frame visualization. Conclusion: Kinovea supports basic motion analysis by providing clear kinematic information and helping beginner athletes observe and refine their movement techniques. The findings also offer practical value for coaches by enabling more precise identification of inefficient patterns and guiding targeted corrections during early-stage training.

title: A Review of Phishing Detection Techniques Using Machine Learning and Natural Language Processing
authors: Dr. Sunita Dixit
journal: Journal of Global Research in Multidisciplinary Studies(JGRMS)
abstract: The goal of phishing attacks, which rank high among cyber risks, is to steal sensitive information (such as login passwords, financial data, and more) from unsuspecting people and companies. Blacklist, whitelist, rule, heuristic, and signature-based detection methods are no longer suitable due to the rising sophistication of phishing schemes. As a result, ML, DL, and NLP are rapidly becoming into effective instruments for detecting both well-known and brand-new forms of phishing. Background on phishing assaults, old ways of detecting them, and recent advances in intelligent phishing detection are all included in this article. It delves into several machine learning algorithms such as decision tree, LSTM, ANN, CNN, and RNN, as well as deep learning models like KNN, NB, and SVM. Also, natural language processing methods including word embedding, sentiment analysis, text categorization, and tokenization are explored with the aim of detecting phishing material. Presenting a comprehensive, precise, and up-to-the-minute phishing detection system is the ultimate goal of this study, which focuses on machine learning frameworks, performance indicators, present obstacles, and future research directions.

abstract: In the context of increasing complexity of modern network infrastructures and the growing number of cyberattacks, improving the effectiveness of intrusion detection systems is a highly relevant task. The aim of this work is to develop and investigate a hybrid approach to network attack detection based on a combination of signature-based analysis and intelligent machine learning methods.  The research methods include analysis of requirements for anomaly detection systems, comparative analysis of existing solutions, design of a hybrid system architecture, and experimental modeling using multiclass classification of network traffic. The results demonstrate that integrating a neural model with a traditional detection system improves attack detection coverage and reduces the number of false positives.  The practical significance of the study lies in the possibility of deploying the proposed architecture in real corporate networks, while the theoretical significance consists in substantiating the effectiveness of a hybrid approach to traffic analysis. Future research directions include adaptive model training and expansion of the range of detectable attacks.

title: Practical Solutions to Common TAVI Complications
authors: Herbert Kroon
abstract: Aortic valve stenosis Calcific aortic valve degeneration mainly affects the elderly population. Approximately 15% of elderly patients have some degree of aortic stenosis (AS)1. Untreated severe AS will lead to heart failure, angina and/or syncope and approximately half of patients will expire within 2 years after symptom onset1, 2. Historically, open heart surgery was the only treatment for severe AS. However, advanced age was a dominant argument to defer surgery. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) was contrived as a less invasive alternative to surgery and to fulfill this unmet clinical need. After the first-in-human procedure in 2002, TAVI matured into a guideline recommended treatment of symptomatic severe AS in elderly patients across the entire risk spectrum3-7. Peri-procedural embolization Operator experience, improved planning and implantation strategies and multiple device iterations including smaller profile, repositioning ability and outer sealing fabric converted TAVI into a reproducible and relatively safe procedure8. However, the “Big Five” of complications in the modern TAVI era remain 1) access site complications and bleedings, 2) paravalvular leakage (PVL), 3) acute kidney injury (AKI), 4) conduction disturbances including the need for permanent pacemaker implantation (PPI) and 5) stroke9. Up to 5% of patients suffer a neurological event after TAVI, mainly within the first 48 hours8, 10, 11. This finding suggests a direct causative role with the transcatheter valve implantation itself. Transcranial Doppler and brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) studies revealed debris embolization towards the brain and new brain lesions after TAVI in the vast majority of patients12-15. Most of these embolizations remain clinically silent at first sight but may be linked to neurocognitive decline and frank dementia16. Embolic protection devices (EPD) have been developed to deflect or capture embolized debris on its way to the brain and may possibly reduce brain lesions and neurological events including stroke and neurocognitive decline. Part I of this thesis adds perspective to the etiopathology of TAVI related stroke and the mechanism of action of the current spectrum of cerebral embolic protection devices. We also present insights into the microscopic analysis of debris that was captured with filters during TAVI procedures. Vascular access and complications 1 TAVI typically requires large bore femoral artery access. By default, larger arteriotomies are at higher risk for access site complications and bleedings. A completely percutaneous approach relies on vascular access closure devices (VCD) to manage the arteriotomy and provide patent hemostasis. TAVI in low to intermediate risk patients is associated with a major vascular complication rate ranging between 2 and 8%4, 11. The conventional closure technique is based on sutures and most access site complications after TAVI procedures are related to closure device failure17. A collagen plug based closure device was introduced as an alternative to sutures. Part II of this thesis addresses vascular complications and provides information on clinical outcomes with collagen plug-based VCD. TAVI-related conduction disturbances Acquired conduction disturbances after TAVI are frequent and may lead to heart failure (re-) admissions and impaired long-term prognosis18-22. The atrioventricular bundle pierces the membranous septum between the right and non-coronary cusp of the aortic valve and surfaces along the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT), which makes it vulnerable to contact pressure by the implanted transcatheter heart valve (THV) during TAVI23, 24. New left bundle branch block (LBBB) and third-degree atrioventricular block (AV3B) requiring PPI occur in up to a third and quarter of patients, respectively18-22. These conduction disturbances may be transient or remain permanent which is clinically relevant in view of in-hospital stay and overall healthcare costs. Unfortunately, there are no uniform definitions to describe conduction dynamics post-TAVI. Inconsistent reporting makes the interpretation of the literature on this topic challenging. Part III of this thesis will elaborate on what is currently known about the incidence of newly acquired conduction disturbances after TAVI and studies specific features on the baseline and postprocedural electrocardiogram (ECG) to predict conduction dynamics. These insights may help determine the need and timing of PPI and adjust hospital discharge policies.

title: Carotid CTA with automated plaque quantification for risk stratification of coexisting obstructive coronary artery disease
authors: Long Jiang Zhang; Minjie Zhao; Changsheng Zhou; JiaNan Li; Sijia Zhao; Jing Li; Hao Tang; Sui Chen; Rui Liu; Wusheng Zhu; Ya Liu; Yun Zhang; 啓吉 金; Wenjing Cui; Pengbo Jiang; Dijia Wu; Xiaoqing Cheng; Zhang Longjiang
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate whether automated carotid plaque quantification on carotid computed tomography angiography (CTA) can serve as an adjunctive risk stratification tool for identifying patients with coexisting obstructive coronary artery disease (OCAD). MATERIALS AND METHODS: This dual-center retrospective study included 2533 adults undergoing paired carotid and coronary CTA within 3 months. Carotid plaque components (calcified, fibrotic, and lipid) were quantified automatically. In the modeling cohort, three diagnostic models for OCAD (stenosis ≥ 50%) were developed using LASSO regression: clinical, plaque, and integrated models. Performance was assessed by AUC (with DeLong's test), decision curve analysis, and calibration curves, with validation in an internal validation set and a temporally independent validation cohort. Sensitivity analysis was performed using severe stenosis (≥ 70%) as the outcome. RESULTS: All carotid plaque volumes were significantly associated with OCAD (p < 0.001). Calcified plaque volume (OR, 2.43; 95% CI: 1.95-3.04) and fibrotic plaque volume (OR, 1.37; 95% CI: 1.01-1.85) were independent predictors. The plaque model achieved an AUC of 0.785 (95% CI: 0.761-0.810) in the training set, comparable to the integrated model (AUC, 0.800) and superior to the clinical model (AUC, 0.723; p < 0.001). Performance remained robust in the internal (AUC, 0.824) and external validation set (AUC, 0.813). The integrated model demonstrated good calibration. Sensitivity analysis yielded consistent results. CONCLUSION: In this retrospective study, automated carotid plaque quantification on CTA provides an adjunctive risk stratification tool to identify patients at high risk for coexisting OCAD, potentially guiding decisions regarding downstream coronary examinations. KEY POINTS: Question Quantitative analysis of carotid plaque components on CTA may help identify patients with OCAD. Findings A model integrating automated carotid plaque volumes and clinical factors effectively identified OCAD. Clinical Relevance This study demonstrates that automated carotid plaque quantification on CTA may serve as an adjunctive risk stratification tool to guide downstream coronary testing in patients with cerebrovascular disease.

title: N-acetylcysteine rescues intracellular Ca2+ signalling and nitric oxide production in human aortic valve endothelial cells from patients with calcific aortic valve stenosis
authors: Pawan Sirwan Faris; Vincenza Valerio; Ilaria Massaiu; Sharon Negri; Giorgia Scarpellino; Valentina Brunetti; Veronika A. Myasoedova; Paolo Poggio; Francesco Domenico Moccia
abstract: Calcific aortic valve stenosis (CAVS), the most common valvular heart disease, is generally regarded as a progressive disease continuum evolving from aortic valve sclerosis (AVSc) to overt aortic stenosis (AS), characterized by increasing leaflet calcification and outflow obstruction. Endothelial dysfunction of the aortic valve plays a crucial role in the pathogenic mechanism leading to CAVS. A remarkable increase in oxidative stress contributes to endothelial injury in CAVS, thereby promoting endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition and impairing endothelium-dependent vasomotion and endothelial barrier function. Endothelial dysfunction can be accompanied by remodelling of the Ca 2+ handling machinery and restoring intracellular Ca 2+ signalling could represent a promising therapeutic strategy to recover endothelial function, including nitric oxide (NO) release. We adopted a multidisciplinary approach (i.e., RNA-seq analysis of Ca²⁺ toolkit-associated genes and single-cell Fura-2 Ca 2+ imaging for intracellular measurements) to investigate for the first time whether the Ca 2+ signalling toolkit is altered in human aortic valve endothelial cells (hVECs) from patients with CAVS (AS-hVECs) compared to VECs from control patients (hVECs; i.e., isolated from patients without stenosis). Bioinformatic analysis revealed that the transcripts encoding inositol-1,4,5-trisphosphate (InsP 3 ) receptors (InsP 3 Rs), i.e., ITPR1 , ITPR2 , and ITPR3 , which mediate Ca 2+ release from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), were not altered, while the transcript encoding the ER Ca 2+ sensor STIM1, which initiates store-operated Ca 2+ entry (SOCE), was up-regulated in AS-hVECs. Capillary Western blot revealed that InsP 3 R and STIM1, but not Orai1 (the main pore-forming subunit of SOCE), proteins were significantly over-expressed in AS-hVECs. Unexpectedly, single-cell Fura-2 Ca 2+ imaging revealed that SOCE, a major driver of endothelial NO release, was remarkably down-regulated in AS-hVECs. Conversely, despite a reduction in the amount of releasable free ER Ca 2+ , physiological Ca 2+ release through InsP 3 Rs was unaffected, reflecting InsP 3 R hyper-responsiveness in AS-hVECs. However, N-acetyl-L-cysteine (NAC), a widely employed ROS scavenger, and the thiol-reducing agent dithiothreitol (DTT) fully rescued SOCE, consistent with the ROS-dependent inhibition of SOCE activation. Furthermore, pre-treatment with NAC also restored acetylcholine-induced NO release. These findings reveal that oxidative stress impairs SOCE in AS-hVECs and identify NAC as a potential therapeutic strategy to prevent endothelial dysfunction in this heart valve disease.

title: Detecting low left ventricular ejection fraction from ECG using an interpretable and scalable predictor-driven framework: a model development and validation study
authors: Ya Zhou; Tianxiang Hao; Ziyi Cai; Haojie Zhu; Hejun He; Jia Liu; Xiaohan Fan; Jing Yuan
abstract: Background Low left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) frequently remains undetected until progression to symptomatic heart failure, underscoring the need for effective approaches to earlier detection of low LVEF. Although artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiography (AI-ECG) has shown promise, existing approaches rely solely on end-to-end black-box models with limited interpretability or on tabular models with limited applicability. Methods In this retrospective multicohort study, we developed and validated a predictor-driven framework that reuses diagnostic scores of conventional ECG findings derived from an ECG foundation model for the detection of low LVEF. The foundation model was developed using 413,167 ECGs from four independent publicly available ECG-only datasets collected across multiple countries, locations, and time periods. The official test set of the EchoNext benchmark, comprising ECG–echocardiography (ECHO) pairs collected at Columbia University Irving Medical Center between 2008 and 2022, was used as the internal test set (n = 5442). We constructed an external test set (n = 16,017) from MIMIC-IV-ECG and related data, comprising ECG–clinical note (Note) pairs collected at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center between 2008 and 2019. The primary outcome was low LVEF (LVEF ≤ 45%), assessed by ECHO or Note documentation within one year after the ECG. The model-derived diagnostic scores for each ECG finding were evaluated for low LVEF discrimination in the internal and external test sets, neither of which was used to develop the ECG foundation model. We further trained tree-based models using these diagnostic representations on the official EchoNext training set (72,475 paired ECG–ECHO records), followed by evaluation on the internal and external test sets. Explainability analyses were performed to identify key predictive features and characterize ECG-related patterns associated with low LVEF. Findings Diagnostic scores for conventional ECG findings showed discriminative performance for low LVEF across cohorts, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) values up to 81.0% for individual predictors. The tree-based model achieved an AUROC of 88.4% (95% confidence interval (CI), 87.1–89.5) in the internal cohort, outperforming the official end-to-end baseline on the EchoNext benchmark, and maintained discrimination in the external cohort, with an AUROC of 86.9% (86.2–87.7). Normal ECG (NORM), incomplete left bundle branch block (ILBBB), and ischemic changes in lateral leads (ISCLA) ranked 1–3 by internal single-predictor AUROC and had the same ranking in the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)–based analysis. Interpretation Diagnostic scores of conventional ECG findings from ECG foundation models contain information relevant to the detection of ventricular dysfunction. These representations can be directly reused for low LVEF detection and further integrated into interpretable predictive models, providing a scalable and extensible computational framework for existing AI-ECG systems. Future research should validate the framework in population-based screening settings and larger international cohorts. Funding This work was partially supported by the CAMS Innovation Fund for Medical Sciences and the National Natural Science Foundation of China.

title: Predictors of mortality in patients treated with ECMELLA after cardiac surgery – a single- center experience
authors: Nizar Salah; Matthias F. Bechtel; Justus Thomas Strauch; Vadim Moustafine; Peter Lukas Haldenwang; Dirk Buchwald; Sebastian Loesaus; Simon Becker; Peter Konrad Zahn; Dinah Maria Berres
abstract: Abstract Background Postcardiotomy cardiogenic shock (PCS) remains a serious complication after cardiac surgery associated with high perioperative mortality. Over the last years, the use of veno-arterial extracorporeal life support (VA-ECLS) combined with left ventricular unloading by a microaxial flow pump (ECMELLA) has increased. Data on mortality predictors in patients treated with ECMELLA for PCS remain limited. We aimed to identify factors associated with 30-day all-cause mortality after ECMELLA implantation. Methods We retrospectively analyzed consecutive patients who received concomitant VA-ECLS and a microaxial pump after cardiac surgery at our university center between 2019 and 2024. Clinically relevant surrogate parameters were assessed along with 30-day mortality. Discriminative ability was assessed by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Survival was analyzed using Kaplan–Meier estimates with log-rank testing, and predictors of 30-day mortality were identified using univariable and multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression. Results Of the 34 patients, 26 (76.5%) died within 30 days. The Model for End-stage Liver Disease (MELD) score was significantly higher in non-survivors than in survivors (18.5 [IQR 10.7] vs. 14.9 [IQR 2.8], p = 0.010). The MELD excluding INR (MELD-XI) score was likewise higher in non-survivors (17.6 [IQR 9.7] vs. 10.2 [IQR 2.6], p = 0.001). Lactate levels were significantly lower in survivors at 12 hours (p = 0.03), 18 hours (p = 0.004) and 24 hours (p = 0.02) after ECMELLA initiation. Discrimination was best at 18 hours (AUC 0.824, p < 0.001). Aortic cross-clamp time was not associated with 30-day mortality when analyzed as a continuous variable; however, an exploratory cutoff of ≥ 63 minutes was associated with increased mortality (HR 3.20, 95% CI 1.34–7.65, p = 0.009). In univariable Cox regression, MELD-XI ≥ 12.5 (HR 2.87, 95% CI 1.13–7.32) and lactate ≥ 2 mmol/L at 18 hours (HR 4.47, 95% CI 1.48–13.52) were associated with 30-day mortality, but neither remained independently associated in multivariable analysis. Conclusions Biological markers, including MELD-XI and lactate, could provide complementary prognostic information before and after ECMELLA implantation, whereas the prognostic value of a prolonged aortic cross-clamp time, observed only in an exploratory threshold analysis, remains uncertain.

title: Extracellular vesicles in viral myocarditis: Mechanisms, biomarkers and emerging therapeutic strategies
authors: Amirhossein Bahreyni; Honglin Luo
abstract: Viral myocarditis (VM) is an inflammatory heart disease most commonly triggered by viral infection and represents a major cause of acute cardiac dysfunction and chronic inflammatory cardiomyopathy. Although cardiomyocyte injury and immune activation are central to VM pathogenesis, the mechanisms by which viral infection coordinates intercellular communication to drive disease progression remain incompletely understood. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as key mediators of cell-to-cell signaling, capable of transporting viral components and host-derived factors that modulate immune responses and cardiac function. In this review, we integrate preclinical and clinical evidence to define the mechanistic roles of EVs in VM and evaluate their translational potential. We highlight circulating EVs as minimally invasive biomarkers for early diagnosis and disease monitoring. We further discuss emerging strategies to therapeutically target or engineer EVs to modulate both viral replication and maladaptive host responses.

title: Advancing cyber-physical systems in surgery through a smart cyber operating theater testbed for medical device integration and clinical translation
authors: Kitaro Yoshimitsu; Ken Masamune; Jun Okamoto; Manabu Tamura; Yoshihiro Muragaki
journal: International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery
abstract: PURPOSE: Operating-room devices and robotic systems are often standalone, which limits synchronized multi-source data utilization and cyber-physical surgical support. This Short Communication presents an integration approach for a Smart Cyber Operating Theater (SCOT) based on OPeLiNK, and reports log-based operational reliability in a clinical SCOT environment. Our focus is the architecture and feasibility of time-synchronized data integration rather than clinical outcome evaluation. METHODS: OPeLiNK was implemented as a common interface and integration architecture consisting of device-specific providers, a data server for management and time synchronization, and application-level data distribution. A university SCOT testbed was established in 2016 for onboarding and integration verification without interrupting clinical workflow. Operational reliability was assessed using de-identified integration logs collected in the clinical SCOT environment (HyperSCOT), defining a successful session as meeting all criteria: required device connection, data reception, application-level display, and time synchronization. RESULTS: The SCOT testbed enabled integration across heterogeneous connections (e.g., Ethernet, serial communication, USB, and video outputs) and supported verification of interconnectivity, including communication validation, data structure consistency, and behavior under abnormal termination and restart. As an application example, a Surgical Strategy Desk was demonstrated using simulated/demo data to show synchronized multi-source visualization. In the clinical environment, SCOT has been used since 2019, including at least 437 glioma surgeries, providing real-world operational logs to support the log-based reliability assessment. CONCLUSIONS: We present an OPeLiNK-based SCOT integration approach and a testbed framework for safe onboarding and verification, complemented by log-based operational evidence from clinical use since 2019. Although clinical effectiveness and efficiency outcomes are out of scope for this Short Communication, reliable time-synchronized integration is a necessary foundation for future cyber-physical operating theaters and advanced decision support applications.

title: sabithav507/FusionGAN-Cardio: FusionGAN-Cardio v1.0.0 – Initial Research Release
authors: sabithav507
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Overview FusionGAN-Cardio is a PyTorch-based research framework for synthetic echocardiographic image generation and quality-controlled data augmentation for cardiovascular disease classification. This initial release provides a modular implementation of a disease- and view-conditioned Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), incorporating multi-level feature fusion, attention mechanisms, anatomical constraints, and synthetic-image quality assessment. Key Features Multi-level gated feature fusion architecture. FiLM-based disease and view conditioning. Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM). Conditional global and patch discriminators. Composite adversarial and structural loss functions. Quality-controlled synthetic image generation. Deficit-driven minority disease-view augmentation. Downstream cardiovascular image classification. Independent generative and anatomical evaluation. Comparative baseline implementations. Statistical analysis and reproducibility utilities. Supported Datasets The implementation provides data preparation and evaluation support for: TMED-2 EchoNet-Dynamic CAMUS Datasets must be obtained independently from their respective official sources. No restricted clinical datasets are included in this release. Evaluation and Validation The framework includes: Medical-feature Fréchet distance and KID. Precision and recall metrics. Optional LPIPS and MS-SSIM. Anatomical Dice and HD95 assessment. Downstream classification metrics. Paired statistical comparisons and study-level bootstrap analysis. Software Contents This release includes: PyTorch source code. Model architecture and training modules. Dataset preparation utilities. Configuration files. Baseline implementations. Evaluation and visualization modules. Unit tests. Non-clinical end-to-end smoke testing. Installation and reproducibility documentation. Installation Install the project dependencies using: pip install -e ".[dev,metrics]" Run software tests using: pytest -q Run the non-clinical smoke test using: fusiongan smoke --workdir outputs/smoke_validation Refer to the README.md for complete installation, dataset preparation, training, augmentation, and evaluation instructions. Important Research Disclaimer This software is intended exclusively for research and educational purposes. Image-level aortic stenosis classification and static-frame ejection-fraction prediction are proxy tasks and must not be interpreted as clinical diagnostic measurements. The release provides an executable research implementation and software verification tests. Real-data experimental results and reproduction of manuscript-reported numerical findings require independent dataset preparation and execution of the prescribed experiments. Release Information Project: FusionGAN-Cardio Version: 1.0.0 Release Type: Initial Research Release Framework: PyTorch License: No software reuse license is specified in this release. Refer to the repository README for licensing information.

title: Surgical and Clinical Insights Into Libman-Sacks Endocarditis of the Mitral Valve: A Case Report and Literature Review
authors: Santiago A. Endara; Gerardo A Dávalos; Daniel A Larrea; Marlon P Aguirre; Patricia Pontón-Villalba; Paula Espinosa Villagomez
abstract: Libman-Sacks, a relatively rare cause of endocarditis, is usually associated with underlying systemic lupus erythematosus and/or antiphospholipid syndrome (APS).In cases of clinical or severe valve regurgitation or stenosis, the treatment approach is to perform a valve replacement or valvuloplasty.We report two cases of young adult male patients with APS who developed Libman-Sacks endocarditis.The first patient is a 38-year-old man, and the second is a 33-year-old man.Both patients had a documented history of thromboembolic events and were receiving anticoagulant therapy.They presented to the emergency department with acute stroke symptoms.The first patient underwent mechanical valve replacement, whereas the second was managed with mitral valvuloplasty.We did a literature review of 10 case reports involving mitral valve replacement and four case reports of mitral valve repair.This literature search extracted demographic, clinical, surgical, and outcome data of 14 patients.Libman-Sacks is an important differential diagnosis when encountering a case of endocarditis with vegetations.We should especially suspect this entity when a patient has an underlying rheumatologic disease.More studies are needed to better comprehend the pathogenesis and treatment of Libman-Sacks.

title: Neuroselective Sensory-Over-Motor Dissociation, Rapid Blockade Onset, and Hemodynamic Autoregulation With 10 μg Intrathecal Dexmedetomidine in High-Risk Orthopedic and Gynecological Surgery: An Observational Analytic Case Series
authors: Muhammad Adiwibowo; Muhamad Farlyzhar Yusuf
journal: Open Access Indonesian Journal of Medical Reviews
abstract: Background: Subarachnoid block gives dense blockade for orthopedic and gynecological surgery, but plain local anesthetics give brief analgesia. Intrathecal dexmedetomidine (DXM), a selective α₂-adrenergic agonist, prolongs block in low-risk patients. Data in high-risk patients are scarce. Objective: To describe block onset, regression, pain scores, and hemodynamic course after 10 μg of intrathecal DXM added to hyperbaric bupivacaine in four high-risk patients. Methods: Four consecutive women (29–73 years) were operated on at Dr. Saiful Anwar Regional General Hospital, Malang, Indonesia (Protocol: CMHC/EC/IRB/2026/0814). Each received 0.5% hyperbaric bupivacaine (15–20 mg) plus 10 μg DXM, by L4–L5 subarachnoid block (Cases 1–3) or combined spinal-epidural anesthesia (Case 4). Onset, hemodynamics, and Numerical Rating Scale (NRS) pain scores were recorded from T₀ to T₄. Results: All patients reached the target block (T6–T10). Sensory onset was ≤ 1 min and Modified Bromage 2 motor block appeared at 3 min; the published mean to Bromage 3 with 5 μg is 11.6 min. Motor inhibition lasted 300 min and analgesia 300–360 min (mean 330 ± 24.5 min), with NRS 0–2 in the first 4 h and 3–4 at 5–6 h. MAP was 70 mmHg in a post-stroke patient. A fall to 50/30 mmHg during bone curettage resolved with 1,000 mL crystalloid and ephedrine. Multimodal and neuraxial analgesia were also given. Conclusion: In four patients, 10 μg of intrathecal DXM was followed by rapid block onset and 5–6 h of analgesia, with no recorded respiratory depression. The series cannot establish effect or mechanism, so controlled studies are needed.

title: Annexins: gatekeepers of endothelial homeostasis and dysfunction
authors: Nerea Méndez‐Barbero; Irene San Sebastián-Jaraba; Hugo Zapata-Polo; María José Fernández-Gómez; Ines Macias-Gamero; José Luis Martín-Ventura; Luis Miguel Blanco‐Colio
abstract: The vascular endothelium plays a central role in maintaining tissue and vascular homeostasis by continuously adapting to biochemical, mechanical, and inflammatory stimuli from its environment. When this adaptive capacity is compromised, endothelial dysfunction develops, driving the onset and progression of a wide range of cardiovascular, metabolic, neurovascular, and inflammatory diseases. Although the molecular mechanisms underlying endothelial dysfunction are complex, growing evidence points to annexins as important regulators of endothelial responses under both physiological and pathological conditions. Annexins are a family of evolutionarily conserved Ca 2+ -dependent phospholipid-binding proteins best known for their roles in membrane organization and cellular signaling. Over the last decade, their functions have expanded considerably, revealing their involvement in processes that are fundamental for endothelial integrity and vascular homeostasis. Emerging studies indicate that annexins influence how endothelial cells respond to inflammatory, oxidative, metabolic, and mechanical stress, thereby shaping vascular barrier function, immune-inflammatory cell recruitment, thrombosis, and tissue repair. In this review, we discuss the current understanding of annexin family members in endothelial biology and examine their contribution to endothelial dysfunction across different disease settings. The available evidence highlights a complex and highly context-dependent network in which individual annexins can either preserve endothelial homeostasis or promote vascular injury depending on the cellular environment and pathological stimulus. A better understanding of their isoform-specific functions may not only advance our knowledge of endothelial pathophysiology but also identify new opportunities for the development of therapeutic strategies targeting inflammatory vascular diseases.

title: Clinical outcomes of TAVI-first versus PCI-first strategies: A meta-analysis of randomized and observational studies
authors: Rodolfo Caminiti; Alfonso Ielasi; Giampaolo Vetta; Antonio Parlavecchio; Dario Pellegrini; Mariano Pellicano; Gabriele Carciotto; Federico Giannino; Andrea Marrone; Davide Besana; Roberto Licordari; Giampiero Vizzari; Antonio Micari
abstract: Background The optimal sequence of transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) remains uncertain. Observational studies suggested lower mortality when PCI was performed after TAVI, but these comparisons may be affected by post-baseline selection. This meta-analysis incorporates the first randomized evidence addressing this question. Methods Randomized and observational studies comparing TAVI-first or PCI after TAVI with PCI-first or PCI before TAVI were included. All-cause mortality was analyzed using adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) from observational studies and an HR approximated from 1-year mortality in the randomized trial. Estimates were pooled using restricted maximum-likelihood random-effects models with Hartung-Knapp inference and stratified by study design. Secondary clinical outcomes were exploratory. Results Six studies were included ( n = 4317): five observational studies ( n = 3331) and one randomized trial ( n = 986). Five studies contributed to the primary mortality analysis, which showed no significant difference between TAVI-first/PCI-after and PCI-first/PCI-before (HR, 0.56; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.20–1.63). Mortality in the randomized trial was 9.5% in both groups. No significant differences were observed for stroke, myocardial infarction, major bleeding, or major vascular complications. Conclusions No mortality advantage was demonstrated for either procedural sequence. In selected patients with stable coronary artery disease and suitable coronary anatomy undergoing balloon-expandable TAVI, TAVI-first appears to be a reasonable alternative to routine upfront PCI, although revascularization and timing should remain individualized. Further direct randomized trials are required.

title: Data underlying the publication: Feasibility of large-scale in silico transcatheter aortic valve implantation trials using a fast-to-evaluate model
authors: Sabine Verstraeten; Marloes van Driel; Robin Willems; Sai Divi; M. J. M. M. Hoeijmakers; Frans N. van de Vosse; Clemens Verhoosel; Wouter Huberts
abstract: This data set contains the data to reproduce the figures from the manuscript: 'Feasibility of large-scale in silico transcatheter aortic valve implantation trials using a fast-to-evaluate model '. The purpose of this study was to assess the feasibility of conducting large-scale in silico TAVI trials using the virtual cohort generator by Verstraeten et al. (2024) in combination with a novel fast-to-evaluate model. This data set contains:1) Matlab scripts to reproduce figures of manuscript.2) Post-processed simulation data needed to reproduce figures of manuscript.3) The 300 male and 450 aortic stenosis .STL geometriesSee the README.txt file for more information about the folders and files in the data set. The simulation data were generated using the novel fast-to-evaluate model that is implemented in Python, as described in the manuscript. The aortic stenosis geometries were generated using the virtual cohort generator, implemented in MATLAB, by Verstraeten et al. (2024). First 300 male and 450 female geometries were generated. The geometries were used as input for the fast-to-evaluate model. Simulations resulting in errors or outliers were discarded. In the end, 200 male and 300 female succesful simulations were used for the analysis of the manuscript. This male/female ratio was equal to the ratio in the clinical trial to which we compared our results.

title: Lipoprotein(a) in Cardiovascular Disease: Integrating Epidemiology, Clinical Guidelines, Molar Measurement, and Emerging Therapies.
authors: Peter E Thomas; Signe Vedel‐Krogh; Florian Kronenberg; Børge Grønne Nordestgaard
abstract: BACKGROUND: Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a causal risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD = myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, peripheral artery disease) and aortic valve stenosis. Plasma concentrations of Lp(a) are >90% genetically determined. Multiple drugs in development reduce lipoprotein(a) by 80% to 98%. While the recently announced topline results, the phase 3 Lp(a)HORIZON trial of pelacarsen did not meet its primary cardiovascular endpoint despite lowering Lp(a), and 3 other cardiovascular outcomes trials remain ongoing. Lipoprotein(a) testing is currently increasing rapidly in many countries. CONTENT: Most guidelines on dyslipidemia and prevention of cardiovascular disease worldwide now advise that Lp(a) should be measured once in all adults, ideally jointly with the first lipid profile ordered. If previous lipid profiles were taken, then Lp(a) should be included in the next lipid profile. Lipoprotein(a) should ideally be measured in nmol/L, and repeat measurements are relevant if drugs are given to lower Lp(a) concentrations, initially at suspected acute coronary syndrome or stroke and again after 1 month, and sometimes in women after menopause. Measuring Lp(a) levels alongside a standard lipid profile provides a more comprehensive initial assessment of a patient's overall cardiovascular risk. Clinical chemistry laboratories that measure lipid profiles should therefore also offer Lp(a) testing. This is easily done as Lp(a) assays can be run on most major clinical chemistry platforms. High Lp(a) is >105 nmol/L (>50 mg/dL). SUMMARY: As use of Lp(a) testing is increasing rapidly worldwide, more clinical chemistry laboratories will likely offer this test locally. Measuring Lp(a) levels alongside a standard lipid profile provides a more comprehensive initial lipid assessment of a patient's cardiovascular risk.

title: Painless Stanford type A aortic dissection presenting with isolated bilateral lower-limb neurological deficits: a case report
authors: Dazheng Fang; Bin Zhao; Jinjie Li; Bing Wu
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Stanford type A aortic dissection (AAD) constitutes a life-threatening cardiovascular emergency. Painless AAD manifesting exclusively as isolated bilateral lower-limb neurological deficits represents an uncommon but recognised presentation of aortic dissection that is prone to misdiagnosis. This case report adds real-world clinical data regarding atypical AAD and delivers practical diagnostic and surgical insights for front-line clinicians. MAIN SYMPTOMS AND IMPORTANT CLINICAL FINDINGS: A 58-year-old Han Chinese female presented with acute-onset bilateral lower-limb numbness and weakness lasting one hour, in the absence of chest, back or abdominal pain. Physical examination uncovered an inter-arm systolic blood-pressure discrepancy together with bilateral lower-limb motor weakness (3/5). Emergency non-contrast chest-abdominal CT identified the aortic double-lumen sign and inward-displaced aortic wall calcified plaques, whereas bilateral distal peripheral pulses remained preserved. MAIN DIAGNOSES, THERAPEUTIC INTERVENTIONS, AND OUTCOMES: Painless Stanford type A aortic dissection complicated by suspected transient spinal cord malperfusion was diagnosed. Following urgent inter-hospital transfer, the patient underwent emergency Bentall procedure combined with aortic arch reconstruction and frozen elephant-trunk graft implantation, with a distal landing zone in the proximal descending thoracic aorta. Her bilateral lower-limb neurological deficits had fully resolved by postoperative day 2. A residual chronic dissection with a thrombosed false lumen persisted distally below the stent-graft and remained stable without interval enlargement. Six-month follow-up confirmed complete functional recovery without residual neurological sequelae or proximal dissection recurrence. CONCLUSION: Undiagnosed painless Stanford type A aortic dissection presenting with isolated bilateral lower-limb neurological deficits is associated with substantial mortality. Routine bilateral upper-arm blood-pressure measurement and recognition of calcification displacement signs on non-contrast CT facilitate early clinical suspicion. Timely confirmation by CTA and urgent comprehensive surgical reconstruction are essential to reverse end-organ malperfusion and optimize neurological as well as survival outcomes.
